note: The Pechenegs — Turkic nomads who occupied the Pontic steppe after the Khazar Khaganate's collapse — were Kiev's most dangerous steppe neighbors in the late 10th century. They besieged Kiev in 968 (forcing Sviatoslav I to return from his Balkan campaigns); they killed Sviatoslav himself at the Dnieper rapids (972) during his return from Bulgaria. Prince Vladimir I (980–1015) built a defensive line of fortresses along the Steppe border. His son Yaroslav 'the Wise' decisively defeated the Pechenegs in 1036, after which they largely dissolved as a political force, replaced by the Cumans.

_quarry.structural_significance: Pecheneg pressure forces Kievan Rus to maintain extensive frontier defenses and limits its military projection into the steppe; Sviatoslav I's death at Pecheneg hands prevents the consolidation of his Rus-Balkan empire; Yaroslav's 1036 victory ends the Pecheneg threat but creates only a brief respite before the Cumans emerge as the new steppe power
